# ROLE
Merge operator. Single objective: integrate oh-my-pi v18.3.0 into the tau
fork using semantic merge drivers, then reconcile Bun resolution. Execute
phases in order. Halt at first failed gate.

# PROHIBITED PATHS
Never read, write, rg, sed, or enumerate:
  ~/.tau/sessions/  ~/.tau/logs/  ~/.tau/cache/  ~/.tau/db/  ~/.tau/run/
  *.jsonl  *.db  *.db-shm  *.db-wal  *.sqlite
  node_modules/  .git/  .bun/  /scratch/
Skip silently. Do not report skips. Rationale: transcripts contain strings
that look like file refs; a prior operator rewrote them and corrupted state.

# WHAT IS TRUE
- Fork packages stay named @oh-my-pi/*. Never rename them.
- @toxicwind/* npm packages do not exist. Overrides to npm:@toxicwind/* 404.
- Correct override shape: { "@oh-my-pi/<pkg>": "workspace:*" }
- Source imports stay @oh-my-pi/*. Never sed them.
- Weave eats false conflicts (different functions, same file). It does not
  resolve genuine entity-modifying conflicts. Verify before trusting it.
- The six permanent divergences are policy, not conflicts. Declare -merge.

# TOOLS (install before use, verify each)
  weave    AST-native entity merge driver   cargo install weave-merge-driver
  suture   format-aware structured merge    cargo install suture-merge-driver
  @gitkraken/conflict-tools   npm, agentic residue loop

# PHASE 0 — Install semantic layer
  cargo install weave-merge-driver 2>&1 | tail -5 || brew install ataraxy-labs/tap/weave
  cargo install suture-merge-driver 2>&1 | tail -5 || brew install wyattau/tap/suture-merge-driver
  weave --version
  suture --version
GATE: both print a version. Else HALT phase=0 TOOLS_MISSING.

# PHASE 1 — Register git merge drivers
  git config --global merge.weave.name "weave entity merge"
  git config --global merge.weave.driver "weave merge %O %A %B %L %P"
  git config --global merge.weave.recursive binary
  git config --global merge.suture.name "suture format merge"
  git config --global merge.suture.driver "suture merge %O %A %B %L %P"
  git config --global merge.suture.recursive binary
GATE: git config --get merge.weave.driver returns the driver string.

# PHASE 2 — .gitattributes in vendor/oh-my-pi
  cd ~/sovereign/projects/tau/vendor/oh-my-pi
  cat >> .gitattributes <<'EOF'
  *.ts   merge=weave
  *.tsx  merge=weave
  *.js   merge=weave
  *.jsx  merge=weave
  *.rs   merge=weave
  *.py   merge=weave
  *.go   merge=weave
  *.json merge=suture
  *.toml merge=suture
  *.yaml merge=suture
  *.yml  merge=suture
  *.md   merge=suture
  crates/pi-builtins/src/bre.rs      -merge
  crates/pi-builtins/src/grep.rs     -merge
  crates/pi-builtins/src/sed.rs      -merge
  packages/ai/src/auth-storage.ts    -merge
  packages/ai/src/auth-storage/**    -merge
  packages/coding-agent/src/debug/** -merge
  EOF
GATE: grep -c merge= .gitattributes > 0.

# PHASE 3 — post-merge hook re-establishing fork intent
  cat > .git/hooks/post-merge <<'EOF'
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  set -euo pipefail
  cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
  rm -f crates/pi-builtins/src/bre.rs
  [ -f packages/ai/src/auth-storage.ts ] && rm -f packages/ai/src/auth-storage.ts
  [ -d packages/coding-agent/src/debug ] && rm -rf packages/coding-agent/src/debug
  echo "[post-merge] permanent divergences re-established"
  EOF
  chmod +x .git/hooks/post-merge

# PHASE 4 — Pre-flight Weave validation (do NOT skip)
  # Weave's benchmark is general OSS. TAU's fork delta is 41k files vs 3.7k
  # upstream — an 11:1 ratio. Validate on 10 files before trusting on 2,953.
  cd ~/sovereign/projects/tau/vendor/oh-my-pi
  FORK_POINT=$(git merge-base HEAD v18.3.0)
  git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U HEAD v18.3.0 2>/dev/null | head -10 > /tmp/sample.txt
  # If no U-files yet, sample from the conflict set:
  git diff --name-only "$FORK_POINT"..HEAD | head -10 > /tmp/sample.txt
  CLEAN=0; TOTAL=0
  while read -r f; do
    TOTAL=$((TOTAL+1))
    git show "$FORK_POINT:$f"  > /tmp/base   2>/dev/null || continue
    git show HEAD:"$f"         > /tmp/ours   2>/dev/null || continue
    git show v18.3.0:"$f"      > /tmp/theirs 2>/dev/null || continue
    if weave merge /tmp/base /tmp/ours /tmp/theirs > /tmp/w.out 2>&1; then
      grep -q '<<<<<<<' /tmp/w.out || CLEAN=$((CLEAN+1))
    fi
  done < /tmp/sample.txt
  echo "weave clean: $CLEAN / $TOTAL"
GATE: if CLEAN < 7, HALT phase=4 WEAVE_INEFFECTIVE. Report the ratio. Fork is
entity-modifying, not entity-additive. The workload is genuinely in the
hundreds; proceed only with explicit human approval.

# PHASE 5 — Merge
  cd ~/sovereign/projects/tau/vendor/oh-my-pi
  git worktree remove /tmp/v18.3.0 --force 2>/dev/null
  git worktree prune
  git merge --no-commit --no-ff v18.3.0 2>&1 | tee /tmp/merge.log
  REMAINING=$(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U | wc -l)
  echo "conflicts after weave+suture: $REMAINING"
GATE: log the number. Do not halt on conflicts — that's the residue.

# PHASE 6 — Residue loop (agentic, per-marker confidence)
  bun add -d @gitkraken/conflict-tools
  cat > /tmp/resolve-residue.ts <<'TS'
  import { parseConflicts, resolveConflicts, refine } from '@gitkraken/conflict-tools';
  import { $ } from 'bun';
  import { readFile, writeFile } from 'fs/promises';
  const conflicted = (await $`git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U`.text())
    .trim().split('\n').filter(Boolean);
  for (const file of conflicted) {
    const content = await readFile(file, 'utf8');
    const digest = await parseConflicts(content, { path: file });
    let resolved = await resolveConflicts(digest, {
      strategy: 'ai',
      context: ['git-blame', 'git-log', 'surrounding-code'],
      minConfidence: 0.85,
    });
    for (let pass = 0; pass < 3; pass++) {
      const findings = await refine(resolved, { path: file });
      if (!findings.some(f => f.severity === 'error')) break;
      resolved = await resolveConflicts(resolved, {
        strategy: 'ai',
        context: ['findings', ...findings],
      });
    }
    if (resolved.verdict === 'clean') {
      await writeFile(file, resolved.content);
      console.log(`CLEAN  ${file}  ${resolved.confidence.toFixed(2)}`);
    } else {
      console.log(`MANUAL ${file}  ${resolved.findings.length} unresolved`);
    }
  }
  TS
  bun run /tmp/resolve-residue.ts 2>&1 | tee /tmp/residue.log
GATE: count MANUAL lines in /tmp/residue.log. Report the number. If > 60,
HALT phase=6 RESIDUE_TOO_LARGE.

# PHASE 7 — Bun reconciliation on merged tree
  cd ~/sovereign/engine
  jq '.overrides = ((.overrides // {}) | with_entries(.value = "workspace:*"))' \
     package.json > package.json.tmp && mv package.json.tmp package.json
  # Ensure root catalog block exists if any dep uses "catalog:"
  rg -l '"catalog:"' packages/*/package.json | wc -l
  # If > 0, copy .workspaces.catalog from v18.3.0 root package.json.
  rm -rf node_modules packages/*/node_modules
  bun install --linker isolated 2>&1 | tail -20
GATE: exit 0.

# PHASE 8 — Verify resolution
  cd ~/sovereign/engine
  bun pm ls 2>/dev/null | grep -c '@oh-my-pi/'
  find . -type l -exec readlink -f {} \; 2>/dev/null | grep -c vendor
GATE: vendor symlink count = 0.

# PHASE 9 — Build and smoke
  timeout 300 bun run build 2>&1 | tail -20
  tau --version
GATE: build exit 0, tau >= 18.3.0.

# RETRY CAP
Any phase: diagnose once, apply one fix, retry once. Second failure -> HALT
with the exact error. No third approach. Thrash rate is the corruption source.

# OUTPUT CONTRACT
Success:
  DONE weave_clean=<n>/10 conflicts=<n> residue=<n> manual=<n> build=ok tau=<ver>

Halt:
  HALT phase=<N> reason=<token> error=<one line>

No narration. No summary. No prose.

new phase `The core issue is that Tau inherits oh-my-pi's truncateHead/truncateTail primitives, and truncateTail has a known defect that directly undermines the tail-truncation strategy for any output whose end is a giant line followed by small lines. This is not a configuration problem — it's a bug in the truncation walker itself.

The defect Tau inherits

Issue #10761 describes it precisely: for large MCP tool results, the tail window collapses to 5 bytes (the envelope's closing } and code fence) out of a 20KB budget. 99.98% of the tail budget goes unused, and the model sees head + elision marker + closing braces, with nothing of the output's actual end.

The defect lives in truncateTail itself, so any caller whose content ends giant-line-then-small-lines is affected. Verified callers include the spill path's tail branch, task executor output, autoresearch experiment tails, broker terminal snapshots, and legacy bash snapshots. Since Tau is a fork of oh-my-pi, it inherits all of this.

Your options, ranked by fit for Tau

1. pi-output-guard — the immediate, lowest-risk fix

This is the most direct answer for Tau because it operates at the universal tool_result event, not on a hardcoded list of tools. It caps every tool result at a configurable token ceiling (default 10,000 tokens). When a result exceeds the ceiling, the full output spills to /tmp/pi-output-guard/ and the LLM sees head + tail + notice with the file path.

The load-bearing detail for your situation: the persisted session JSONL is never touched. That's the exact failure mode from the prior incident — the agent rewriting session transcripts it mistook for dependents. pi-output-guard cannot cause that corruption because it only mutates the in-flight tool_result content delivered to the LLM. It also provides an output_read tool so the model can pull specific sections from the spilled file instead of reaching for | head.

The tradeoff: it's a plugin, not a fork-level fix. You install it via pi install git:https://github.com/26q5gr9hwd-crypto/pi-output-guard, and it runs automatically. No engine code changes required.

2. Patch truncateTail in the Tau fork — the durable fix

Since Tau is a fork, you can fix the underlying walker. The bug is in streaming-output.ts around lines 419–484, where the tail walker fails to handle the giant-edge-line case correctly. The elider's own intent comment says a giant first/last line should be byte-windowed: "A giant first/last line cannot use one of the line-preserving windows. Use a byte window only for that side" — but the implementation doesn't do that for the tail side.

This is the correct long-term fix because it repairs the primitive for all callers, not just the ones that happen to route through a plugin. It also means Tau's fork actually diverges from upstream in a way that fixes a real bug, rather than papering over it.

3. Tau's own session repair mechanism — already present, but defensive

Tau already has a tau.session-history-repair custom entry that appends a repaired branch instead of rewriting the JSONL file. The original entries remain untouched, and the agent loop repairs its own history by appending rather than mutating. This is the right architecture, but it's a recovery mechanism, not a prevention mechanism. It stops new corruption from making sessions unusable, but it doesn't stop the agent from trying to rewrite the session in the first place. pi-output-guard is what stops the attempt.

What I'd actually do

Install pi-output-guard first. It takes five minutes, requires no code changes, covers every tool including MCP and custom ones, and explicitly never touches the session JSONL. That solves the immediate truncation problem and removes the agent's incentive to reach for | head because the full output is always retrievable via output_read.

Then patch truncateTail in the fork. The upstream issue is open and unfixed. Since you control the fork, you can fix the walker to byte-window the tail side when the edge line is oversized. That's the difference between "Tau works around an inherited bug" and "Tau fixes an inherited bug."

Do not rely on prompt-level instructions alone. Telling the agent "don't use | head" is a nudge, not a constraint. The harness has to make truncation structurally unnecessary — which is exactly what pi-output-guard does by capping the result and spilling the full version. `

You're right — I was answering the wrong question. You asked what exists and what to use, and I gave you a risk lecture instead of a survey. Here's what's actually out there, and how it fits together for someone who wants the agent to act as a competent engineer on their own machine.

The core split: two merge drivers, one agentic residue loop, one Bun reconciliation

The Weave/Suture/GitKraken stack maps onto three different merge populations, each with its own tool:

Population Tool Mechanism
Code (TS/JS/Rust/Python/Go) Weave Entity-level merge via tree-sitter. Functions, classes, methods merged as units.
Structured config (JSON/YAML/TOML/MD) Suture Format-aware merge. JSON keys, YAML mappings, TOML tables merged structurally.
Residue (real semantic collisions) GitKraken conflict-tools Agentic AI loop with git context (blame, grep, diff, log).

Weave's own benchmark claims 31/31 clean merges vs Git's 15/31 on a 31-scenario cross-language suite, with zero regressions across real merge commits from git/git, CPython, Flask, Go, and TypeScript repos . The mechanism is straightforward: parse base/ours/theirs into semantic entities, match by identity (name + type + scope), merge at the entity level. Different entities changed = auto-resolved. Same entity changed by both = attempt intra-entity merge. That's exactly the failure mode you hit: an agent adding bar() while another modifies foo() in the same file is a false conflict under line-based merge, and Weave eats it .

Suture covers 17+ structured formats — JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, SQL, Markdown, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, SVG, RSS/Atom, iCalendar, OTIO, .properties/.ini . It installs as a git merge driver in 5 seconds via a curl script, or via Homebrew/npm/PyPI/Cargo . For a Tau/oh-my-pi merge where bun.lock, package.json, tsconfig.json, and .github/workflows/ci.yml all conflicted, Suture is the tool that keeps both sides' keys instead of forcing you to pick one.

GitKraken conflict-tools is the residue handler. It has three entry points: extractConflict() (parse-only, no AI), resolveConflict() (single-file AI loop), and resolveConflicts() + applyResolutions() (batch every unmerged file, stage results) . It runs an agentic loop that calls git tools (blame, grep, diff, log, show, readFile) and writes resolved content back to the working tree. The defaultVerifier scans for residual conflict markers during the loop and retries with feedback on failure . Confidence scores per resolution; you gate at 0.85 and route anything below to manual review.

What this changes for the Tau merge specifically

Your 2,953 "conflicts" were an artifact of line-based merge applied to an 11:1 fork-to-upstream ratio. Weave's own validation says the tool resolves false conflicts and leaves real semantic collisions. The residue after Weave + Suture should be in the low hundreds, not 2,953. The agentic loop then handles most of what's left.

The reason this matters for your specific case: the tau fork has 41k changed files against upstream's 3.7k. That's not normal drift — it's wholesale restructuring. Weave's benchmark is on general OSS, not on a fork this divergent. The pre-flight validation gate in the prompt (sample 10 files, require ≥7 clean) is what catches the case where Weave doesn't help because the fork is entity-modifying rather than entity-additive.

The yolo/agent-as-you ecosystem

For an agent that acts as you on your own machine, the relevant settings and plugins:

omp itself ships with yolo as the built-in default approval mode . omp --approval-mode=yolo acp gives the agent full read/write/exec without prompts. --auto-approve and --yolo force it per-session. The docs are explicit about the tradeoff: "Use an explicit yolo mode, then deny or prompt capabilities the job should not exercise" . You can scope it — deny specific bash patterns, deny per-tool — while keeping the rest unrestricted.

omp-smart-approve is the interesting counterpoint. It doesn't add friction for the calls you want to auto-approve; it audits the ones that run silently because the tool is on an auto-approve list or the session is in yolo mode or a subagent inherited a permissive setting . For an agent acting as you, this is the log you actually want — not permission gates, but a record of what ran and why it was allowed.

pi-output-guard directly addresses the truncation problem. It hooks the universal tool_result event and caps every tool result at 10,000 tokens. When a result exceeds the ceiling, the full output spills to /tmp/pi-output-guard/ and the LLM sees head + tail + a notice with the file path . It also provides an output_read tool so the model can pull specific sections from the spilled file instead of reaching for | head. The load-bearing detail for your situation: the persisted session JSONL is never touched. It only mutates the in-flight tool_result content delivered to the LLM.

pi-promptsmith is the prompt compiler. Its own description: "Intent-aware prompt rewriter and execution-contract compiler for Pi" . Two modes: plain rewrite (clarify, tighten) and execution contract (turn a rough task into an agent-executable spec with goal, context, constraints, files to inspect, expected change, verification steps, output expectations). The auto mode uses deterministic heuristics to decide which mode a draft gets.

pi-tasks is the runtime counterpart: "evidence-gated completion, ordered plans, compaction-safe resume" . Agents cannot mark work done without traceable, reproducible proof. Vague or compound steps are rejected; non-atomic steps must be broken down before execution. This is what stops the agent from declaring DONE build=ok tau=18.3.0 without actually showing the build output.

The truncateTail bug you're working around

Issue #10761 is real and unfixed upstream. The tail window collapses to 5 bytes (the envelope's closing braces) out of a 20KB budget because the walker reaches the giant payload line with includedLines === 2 — the MCP envelope guarantees two tiny lines after the payload — and the byte-window fallback is gated on includedLines === 0 . The break path forfeits the entire remaining tail budget . Affected callers include the spill path's tail branch, task executor output, autoresearch experiment tails, broker terminal snapshots, legacy bash snapshots, and advisor/ask context packing .

The fix is to byte-window the oversized edge line regardless of includedLines, using the full maxBytes budget when no complete lines have been included yet. The comment already says this should happen: "A giant first/last line cannot use one of the line-preserving windows. Use a byte window only for that side" . The implementation just doesn't do it for the tail side.

What I'd actually run, in order

```
# 1. Install the merge stack
brew install ataraxy-labs/tap/weave
brew install WyattAu/suture-merge-driver/suture-merge-driver
npm i -g @gitkraken/conflict-tools

# 2. Wire them as git merge drivers
weave setup          # writes .gitattributes for supported code types
suture driver install # writes .gitattributes for structured formats

# 3. Pre-flight: sample 10 files from the conflict set
#    If Weave clean-merges <7/10, the fork is entity-modifying
#    and the residue loop is the primary tool, not Weave.

# 4. Run the merge with drivers active
git merge --no-commit --no-ff v18.3.0 --allow-unrelated-histories

# 5. Residue loop on whatever survives
#    Write the @gitkraken/conflict-tools batch resolver
#    with minConfidence: 0.85 and defaultVerifier.

# 6. Bun reconciliation
cd ~/sovereign/engine
# overrides: { "@oh-my-pi/<pkg>": "workspace:*" }  — NOT npm:@toxicwind/*
# catalog: copy .workspaces.catalog from v18.3.0 root package.json
bun install --linker isolated

# 7. Patch truncateTail in the fork
#    engine/packages/coding-agent/src/session/streaming-output.ts
#    Byte-window the oversized tail edge line using full maxBytes
#    when includedLines === 0, and don't break when it's > 0.

# 8. Verify
tau --version
bun pm ls | grep -c @oh-my-pi/
find . -type l -exec readlink -f {} \; | grep -c vendor
```

For the yolo side: omp --approval-mode=yolo is already the default. The plugins that matter are pi-output-guard (truncation + session safety), pi-promptsmith (execution contracts), and pi-tasks (evidence gates). omp-smart-approve if you want an audit trail without adding friction.

The thing I got wrong before was treating the security posture as the point. It isn't. The point is that the agent should be able to do the work, and the tooling should make the work verifiable without making it slower.
